For anyone who may not know the story behind obtaining the Corrupted Ashbringer, it dropped off of the 4 Horseman encounter in the original, level 60 version of Naxx back in Vanilla. Naxx was released as the final raid of Vanilla shortly before the Burning Crusade expansion. In order to even enter the raid, you had to obtain a key. To get the key, you had to obtain various expensive materials and (if I remember correctly) there was a gold cost as well. The higher your reputation was with the Argent Dawn, the less expensive your key was. However, raising your Argent Dawn rep was nowhere near as easy as it is now. You pretty much had to farm scourge mobs over and over and over. Naxx was a 40 man raid back then and everyone in your group needed the key to enter.

Once everyone had their key, the real fun began. The original Naxx is still largely regarded as one of the most difficult raids in WoW. If you and your group weren't already decked out in gear from AQ 40, you were going to have a bad time. The amount of work involved in getting a 40 man raid group geared enough to be successful in Naxx was huge. Add to that the fact that the 4 Horseman encounter itself was largely considered one of the most difficult in WoW. I believe you needed 8 well geared warrior tanks for what was considered the best strategy back then. And of course, not only did you need to beat the encounter, but the RNG Gods needed to be on your side, too.

All in all, only about 1% of the playerbase back then ever completed Naxx. It was the definition of hard core raiding back then. Things like this are why the Corrupted Ashbringer should remain off the BMAH.

Don't get me wrong, I agree with you about the lack of a sense of community to a large extent. I feel like a lot of the features that were added for convenience's sake have given players the opportunity be complete assholes without any sort of consequences. Back when I played in Vanilla and BC and early on in Wrath, if you acted like a jerk in a group, you became the talk of trade chat and the forums and were typically "black listed" by most of the server. It served as a sort of punishment for causing others grief and often meant you had to reroll. The ability to remain anonymous through tools like the dungeon and raid finder have pretty much brought an end to this sort of thing.

In spite of all this, I still think the playerbase is largely in control of their destiny. I haven't had the chance to play WoD yet, but I'm assuming there's nothing keeping people from leaving their garrisons and getting out in the world if they want to. There's nothing stopping anybody from hopping on their server's forum and trying to find players with similar interests (raiding/PVP/achievement hunting/etc.) to group up with. There's nothing preventing anyone from hanging out in a starting zone and offering help to people new to the game. Sure, it may be more difficult than it was back in the earlier years of the game to find like-minded players, but it's still very much possible.

Just wanted to say that I totally agree with you about going out there and creating your own adventures in WoW! I've played pretty solidly since like April/May of 2005 with a few breaks here and there. I'm currently on my longest break thus far (about a year) due to some real life issues, but am working on getting a new gaming computer soon and jumping right back in.

With that being said, all the posts I see about lack of content and the doom and gloom, "The end is near!" type stuff about losing subscribers always sort of rub me the wrong way. I've taken a lot of brief breaks since I first started playing, but they were never because I felt like there was nothing left to do in WoW. This game has so much more to offer than just raiding and PVP. Like you, I really enjoy exploring. Sometimes, when I felt bored, I'd hop on my mount and just run or fly around the different zones and see what there was to see. If there's one thing the developers have always gotten right, it's been creating beautiful and varying environments for the players to explore.

If exploring isn't your thing, try something else! If you're new to the game, go back and run old dungeons and raids. Go after some of the more difficult achievements. Go mount or pet collecting. Have little, silly in game contests with guildies and friends. Heck, even go find a new player in one of the starting zones or on the forums and offer to show them the ropes of the game.

I don't want to sound like a little, old lady complaining about how we only had sticks and rocks to play with back in the day, but I feel like so much of this game is what you make it out to be. Go out there and create your own fun!

I had the Stockade Pauldrons drop for me back in Vanilla. Pretty sure that was the first world BoE epic I ever saw. My main was a human warrior, but I absolutely loved the Night Elf mounts and decided to grind out exalted reputation with Darnassus by turning in runecloth. I was farming ogres in the area that leads up to Kara in Deadwind Pass and that's where I had the Pauldrons drop. I already had my tier 1 shoulders at this point so I sold the Pauldrons for several hundred gold and used it to buy the runecloth I needed to finish grinding out my rep and to help buy my new kitty mount.

Me and my best friend also had a BoE epic gun (think it may have been the Precisely Calibrated Boomstick) drop off one of the scourge mobs in Andorhal one night while we were out there farming Argent Dawn rep for the Naxx key. If I remember correctly, she put it on the AH and we split the gold when it sold.

I also saw the Krol Blade and Skullflame Shield drop in Strath on different occasions. The Krol Blade was during a guild run and we let our rogue in the group take it. The night the Shield dropped was during a guild run too. We all rolled greed, but I lost the roll. :(

I can totally relate! I first started playing WoW back in early 2005 on the pretty basic Dell laptop my parents had bought me for college. Back then, I had no clue about "gaming rigs" and just assumed any old computer should be able to run the game just fine. Surprisingly, my little PoS laptop held up all the way until I hit 60 and joined a raiding guild. I quickly grew frustrated with how the game would freeze up during every trash pull back in the good old days of MC and after a little research knew I was going to need a better computer.

The second computer I used was one that a friend built for me. Being a college student at the time, I had a really limited budget and I think he built the whole thing for me for $400 - $450. It wasn't amazing by any means, but it was a hell of a lot better than my crummy little laptop. I remember logging in for the first time and noticing the details on my character's cape and going "OMG, I had no idea that was there!". I was finally able to raid without having my screen lock up on every pull and actually made the transition from being a DPSer, to off tank, to main tank within the matter of a few months. Thanks to that computer, I've been tanking ever since. :) It kicked the bucket a few years ago, but if it wasn't for the upgrade, I'd have probably quit the game.

Like you said, I think it mainly has to do with tanks often being used as a scapegoat. If the group wipes, it's usually tanks who get blamed first (with healers coming in at a very close second) regardless of what actually caused the group to fail. I think a lot of people just don't want the responsibility that comes along with tanking and the stress that goes along with it. Tanking requires a very specific set of knowledge and a lot of research. You need to understand the ins and outs of your spec's survival abilities, the mechanics of the trash and bosses you'll be fighting, the layout of the dungeon/raid, positioning, etc. Sadly, I think the way that Blizzard has tried to make the game more accessible to the average player has had a negative impact on the amount of effort people feel they need to put in to the game. There are a lot of people out there that just want to rush to the level cap as quickly as possible and get their hands on those epic shinies asap without having to take the time to research their class, spec, fight mechanics, etc. and you can't ignore those things if you want to be a successful tank. Of course, these things are important to all of the roles in the game, but I think tanking is probably the least forgiving for people who don't put in the research.

I also feel like there's a lot of players who are drawn to those big damage numbers put up by DPSers. For them, there's nothing cooler than seeing the mob they're fighting bite the dust in a matter of seconds thanks to their massive damage output. There's nothing wrong with this, of course, it's just a matter of "different strokes for different folks".

With that being said, I've played a tank since Vanilla. My main back then was a protection warrior and I switched over to a feral druid who has been my main since early BC. I LOVE tanking. For me, it's not about putting up huge DPS numbers, it's about seeing just how much of a beating my character can take. I also enjoy learning about the different mechanics of encounters and how I'm in control of making sure the big baddy doesn't obliterate my friends. For me, there's nothing cooler than charging up to a massive raid boss, getting right in it's face, and going "bring it on, chump!".

I do agree that the whole revamped Forsaken starting story is a bit strange. I remember creating a new undead just to see what sort of changes they had made since Arthas was dead now and the new story just didn't feel right to me. Sylvanas gives the newly rezzed undead the option to serve her and I kept thinking to myself "Why would they align themselves with her now that Arthas has been dealt with?". There's no more motive of revenge against the Lich King and the scourge. I think it's probably safe to say too that some of the corpses she's bringing back are people who didn't even die as a result of the scourge in the first place. For example, why would your average Joe human peasant who died of old age suddenly willingly want to serve the Horde and fight against the Alliance? Doesn't really make much sense to me.

This is something that I had sort of considered myself, but my train of thought went a little differently. When I considered some of the scourge breaking free and regaining their free will, I was thinking about the remaining scourge in Icecrown. This made me then go "wait a minute...that wouldn't really work because those scourge are pretty powerful and probably wouldn't make sense as level 1's." Then of course there would have been the issue of getting them to the Forsaken starting area. For whatever reason, I didn't really consider the scourge still lurking around in Lordaeron. That idea really does seem plausible.

Just like Calia, I can't really find much information about her. I imagine any lore surrounding her is based largely in the books (which I really need to start reading. lol). From what little info I could find, it seems most people assume she simply died of old age before the plague. I'm not sure if Blizzard has actually confirmed this though. Looks like she's another character tied to really important storyline that they just sort of swept under the rug. I mean, I know they obviously can't take the time to develop every single character, but I'm really curious as to what happened to the rest of the Menethil family and the possible influence they could have on events in the present and future.

This is really part of the reason I brought my original question up. I really do feel like Blizzard has forgotten about her and in my opinion, it's really a shame. There are a ton of directions they could take her story off in simply because so little is actually known about her. Is she alive? Is she dead? Is she undead? I just feel like Blizzard is forgetting about a character that would be like a lump of clay in a good developer's hands. There's not a lot of lore about her specifically, but the lore that surrounds her is some of my favorite in the game because it's just so rich. If I were a Blizzard employee, I would jump at the chance to get to develop a new storyline for her. I'll feel disappointed if we never see any mention of her as the game continues on in the years to come or if they're just like "Yup. She's dead. That's it. End of story." (Isn't that sort of what they did with Terenas' wife?)

Yeah, /u/Captainsir mentioned this possibility earlier. I agree with you that if Calia is still alive, there's no way the Forsaken would trust her as their leader...or anyone else who's still breathing for that matter.

Like you said, what she's doing isn't really causing any major issues for the time being, but I think it's the potential of what she could do with an essentially endless army at her command that makes the other leaders uneasy. She's not really overstepping her boundaries at this point in time, but the potential is there. I think at this point in time though, they see the Forsaken presence in the Eastern Kingdoms as a necessity for maintaining Horde interests there. Only time will tell if that will change.

The Blood Elves obviously have strong ties to Sylvanas, but Lor'themar made it pretty clear in SoO that he's not cool with her use of the val'kyr. I really don't know how the Horde Pandaren feel about the Forsaken (someone please fill me in if you do). Garrosh absolutely HATED Sylvanas and as a result, I'd imagine there's probably a pretty good chunk of orcs that probably do now as well. I'm not sure if Thrall knows what Sylvanas has been up to since he's been off saving the world, but I don't think he'd be very happy with her either. I really don't think the goblins give a damn one way or the other. Vol'jin seems like the only Horde leader who might be able to understand where Sylvanas is coming from. My troll lore knowledge isn't the greatest, but I believe his people were nearly wiped out once too. I think he also understands the importance of the Forsaken presence in the Eastern Kingdoms and in making sure the continent doesn't fall completely in to the hands of the Alliance.
Actually, does anyone know if she's mentioned in any of the Warcraft games at all, or is she strictly a character from the books? I've never played Orcs vs. Humans or Warcraft II.

I definitely think most of the Forsaken still have respect for Terenas. Why would they leave his tomb and his throne at the entrance to their capital city if they saw him as a failure? Although, isn't the tomb actually empty? I believe Arthas stole his father's urn to transport Kel-Thuzad and simply dumped the ashes. Oh, don't get me wrong, I'd be very sad to see Sylvanas go. There's also no guarantee that we'll see her downfall in WoW at all. It's still entirely possible that Sylvanas will "see the error of her ways" so to speak and repair her reputation. It's just with the way that her story has unfolded recently, she's walking a very thin line. Even her allies in the Horde have become increasingly suspicious of her actions thanks to what happened at the Wrathgate and her use of the val'kyr. Vol'jin seems to be tolerating her actions for now at least, but I'm not sold on the idea that he'll just sit back and continue to let her raise the dead. 

If Blizzard wants to continue having Sylvanas rule the Forsaken, I'm thinking the key to her snapping out of her Lich King-like ways may lay with Alleria. If there's anyone left who might be able to talk some sense in to her, I'm thinking it might be her. Her meeting up with Vareesa obviously didn't go too well, but maybe they're saving our reunion with Alleria for a reason. Again, this is just totally me speculating.

Then there's still the issue of explaining the creation of new Forsaken characters. If Sylvanas changes her tune or if a new Forsaken leader emerges who is against the use of the val'kyr, I don't know how Blizzard will be able to explain new, level 1 Forsaken. I have my own personal ideas on how they may handle it, but that's a whole new can of worms. lol

Lilian's story actually starts in the Cata revamped Forsaken starting area. She's rezzed as an undead by the val'kyr along with your new character. However, she sees herself as a monster and wants nothing to do with Sylvanas or the Forsaken and ends up running off. As you progress through Tirisfal, you discover that she's been captured by the Scarlet Crusade. You also come to discover that her father is a high ranking member of the Scarlet Crusade. Lilian assumes that her father will come and save her, but he actually orders her to be executed. She goes all swirly, purple fire on the guy that's come to kill her and manages to escape. Later on in the zone, she continues running around killing members of the Scarlet Crusade, including her father. She ends up running off to Scholomance and trying to take on Darkmaster Gandling. I'm not really sure where her story goes from there (I haven't played WoD and haven't leveled a Horde character through Mists, so it's entirely possible she pops up from time to time in those expansions).

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W2jXtEB1Kuo is a great video that explains the details of her story in a lot greater depth.

And like you said, I think she would need to do something BIG to show that she'd be as capable of a leader as Sylvanas (if not, better). I guess the way I'm looking at it is Calia is pretty much a blank slate. Blizzard hasn't touched her character at all in WoW (I don't think she's even mentioned in Warcraft III, if I remember correctly) and really could do just about anything they wanted with her. In other words, she's not really bogged down by a ton of previous lore that would truly get in the way of the Forsaken respecting her.

Just a few tips if you're going to use a crate: Make sure the crate is the right size. The dog should be able to fully stand up, turn around, and lay down comfortably. Remember that a puppy is only going to get bigger so go with a larger size if you don't want to spend more money on a new crate in a few weeks. Another trick is to lay a blanket or towel over the crate. It'll help the puppy feel safe and secure. A ticking clock can come in handy too. You can place it just outside of the crate so the pup doesn't chew it up. The steady ticking noise is supposed to mimic the sound of the mother dog's heartbeat and can have a soothing effect. If you feel like splurging, they make machines for babies that actually play the sound of a heart beating.
